R Notebook

Inputs: fastq files

Completed on dada version 1.30 and phyloseq version 1.46.0

Check the version of dada2 you have installed, if you have a version of dada2 that is less than 1.4, you will need to find the tutorial for your version and check if the dereplication step can be skipped: I’m using version 1.26.0 so I will need to follow the old Dada2 tutorial. The main difference is that in the new tutorial you can skip the dereplication step, which is helpful if your computer has low memory. Here is the current dada2 tutorial.

Basic steps:

STEPS

  • Step 1: Getting the files ready

  • Step 2: Quality assessment and filtering

    • Step 2.1: Filtering & Trimming Primers or low quality sections of data
    • Step 2.2: Checking quality after filtering

  • Step 3: Dereplication step

  • Step 4: Error rates

  • STEP 5: Construct ASVS with DADA2

  • Step 6: Make a sequence table and remove chimeras

  • Step 7: Assign taxonomy

  • Step 8: Load metadata

  • Step 9: Assemble phyloseq objects

Optionally you can make a tree and add it to your phyloseq object. I don’t have a tree making step in this workflow, but just know it is an option.

Note that most of the code here is commented out, and I’ve saved the objects that were made using the saveRDS function. This way if I need to stop mid-way, I won’t lose my progress. I can then re-load the made object with the readRDS function. Several of these steps require significant computational capacity and you won’t want to have to re-run them every time because they take a lot of time to run.

library(tidyverse)

library(readxl)
library(ggpubr)
library(phyloseq)
library(janitor)
## 
## Attaching package: 'janitor'
## 
## The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
## 
##     chisq.test, fisher.test
library(dada2)
## Loading required package: Rcpp

set up file paths

First we set up the file path to where your fastq sequences are

path <- "../data/data"

#check that your data files are listed in the path, if not, you probably set the file path wrong
list.files(path)

Then, we have to tell R which samples are the forward reads and which samples are the reverse reads

# Forward and reverse fastq filenames have format: SAMPLENAME_R1_001.fastq and SAMPLENAME_R2_001.fastq
fnFs <- sort(list.files(path, pattern="_R1_001.fastq", full.names = TRUE))
fnRs <- sort(list.files(path, pattern="_R2_001.fastq", full.names = TRUE))

# Extract sample names, assuming filenames have format: SAMPLENAME_XXX.fastq
sample.names <- sapply(strsplit(basename(fnFs), "_"), `[`, 1)

Filter and Trim to remove primers and low quality reads

You will need to know what your primer sequences are so that you can trim them.

The primers for this project are 515F modified and 806R modified Walters et al. 2016

515f Modified GTGYCAGCMGCCGCGGTAA 806r Modified GGACTACNVGGGTWTCTAAT

  • trimLeft should be set to the lengths of the forward and reverse primers
  • truncLen Truncate reads after trunLenc

Dereplication

Dereplication combines all identical sequencing reads into into “unique sequences” with a corresponding “abundance” equal to the number of reads with that unique sequence. Dereplication substantially reduces computation time by eliminating redundant comparisons.

Dereplication in the DADA2 pipeline has one crucial addition from other pipelines: DADA2 retains a summary of the quality information associated with each unique sequence. The consensus quality profile of a unique sequence is the average of the positional qualities from the dereplicated reads. These quality profiles inform the error model of the subsequent sample inference step, significantly increasing DADA2’s accuracy.

errF <- readRDS("output/errF")
errR <- readRDS("output/errR")

The error rates for each possible transition (A→C, A→G, …) are shown. Points are the observed error rates for each consensus quality score. The black line shows the estimated error rates after convergence of the machine-learning algorithm. The red line shows the error rates expected under the nominal definition of the Q-score. * Estimated error rates (black line); observed rates (points)

plotErrors(errF, nominalQ=TRUE)

Construct seq tab

Once we have our merged sequences, we construct a sequence table. The sequence table contains all of the unique 16S sequences and the counts for each of the sequences in each sample.

# seqtab <- makeSequenceTable(mergers)
# dim(seqtab)
# 
# saveRDS(seqtab, "output/seqtab")

seqtab <- readRDS("output/seqtab")

Considerations for your own data: Sequences that are much longer or shorter than expected may be the result of non-specific priming. You can remove non-target-length sequences from your sequence table (eg. seqtab2 <- seqtab[,nchar(colnames(seqtab)) %in% 250:256]). This is analogous to “cutting a band” in-silico to get amplicons of the targeted length. (dada2 tutorial)

# Inspect distribution of sequence lengths
table(nchar(getSequences(seqtab)))
## 
##  160  168  178  180  215  221  232  233  249  251  252  253  254  255 
##   96    1    1    1    5    1    1    1    1    2 3502 7809  264   21
#some sequences are shorter than expected. I am going to remove any sequences less than 250 bp

seqtab <- seqtab[,nchar(colnames(seqtab)) %in% 250:256]

#check sequences again after filtering
table(nchar(getSequences(seqtab)))
## 
##  251  252  253  254  255 
##    2 3502 7809  264   21

Remove chimeras

A sequencing chimera is a type of artifact that occurs during the process of DNA sequencing, specifically during the Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) amplification process. These chimeras are formed when two or more distinct DNA sequences are incorrectly joined together, producing a sequence that does not naturally exist in the organism being studied. (GPT -4o)

#seqtab.nochim <- removeBimeraDenovo(seqtab, method="consensus", multithread=TRUE, verbose=TRUE)

#saveRDS(seqtab.nochim, "output/seqtab.nochim")

seqtab.nochim <- readRDS("output/seqtab.nochim")

Track reads through pipeline

#check number of reads that made it through each step of the pipeline

getN <- function(x) sum(getUniques(x))
track <- cbind(out, sapply(dadaFs, getN), sapply(dadaRs, getN), sapply(mergers, getN), rowSums(seqtab.nochim))
# If processing a single sample, remove the sapply calls: e.g. replace sapply(dadaFs, getN) with getN(dadaFs)
colnames(track) <- c("input", "filtered", "denoisedF", "denoisedR", "merged", "nonchim")
rownames(track) <- sample.names
head(track)

Make phyloseq object

Load metadata. The important thing is to make sure that the the rownames of the seqtab are identical to the rownames of the metadata

In my case, the rownames do not match with the sample_id [1] “SG001-G001” “SG002-G002” “SG003-G003” “SG004-G004” “SG005-G005” “SG006-G006” “SG007-G007” [1] “G0001” “G0002” “G0003” “G0004” “G0005” “G0006” “G0007”

Need to remove the SG… From the rownames, and then remove an extra 0 from the sample names

First load the metadata file

# Using sub() to replace everything up to and including the first "-"
rownames(seqtab.nochim) <- sub(".*-", "", rownames(seqtab.nochim))

meta.df <- read_csv("meta_edit2.csv")
## Rows: 537 Columns: 18

## chr (8): sample_id, mouse_cage, sample_specimen, collection_date, location, ...
## dbl (4): collection_time, mouse_death_date, mouse_experiment_day, mouse_diet...
## lgl (6): study_id, mouse_id, day_post_abx, fmt_y_n, host_id, blood_glucose_m...

meta.df <- as.data.frame(meta.df)

#make sample id the rownames for the metadata 
rownames(meta.df) <- meta.df$sample_id 

#see if there are differences between the two objects
#diff <- setdiff( rownames(meta.df), rownames(seqtab.nochim)) 
#diff <- setdiff( , rownames(seqtab.nochim), rownames(meta.df)) 


#check if identical
identical(rownames(seqtab.nochim), rownames(meta.df))
## [1] TRUE

Now we put all the pieces together in a phyloseq object: the seqtab, the metadata, and the taxa table

#should be true
identical(colnames(seqtab.nochim), rownames(taxa)) 
## [1] TRUE
ps <- phyloseq(otu_table(seqtab.nochim, taxa_are_rows=F), 
               sample_data(meta.df), 
               tax_table(taxa))

ps
